stories.title: Singapore Airlines Adds Extra Flights to Rescue Stranded Travellers
stories.headline_kid: Singapore Airlines is running extra flights to Jakarta to help thousands of people who got stuck when a volcano's ash grounded planes!
summary: Remember the volcano that erupted in Indonesia last week? Its ash cloud was so thick that eight airports, including Jakarta's main airport, had to shut down. That meant almost 3,000 flights were cancelled and more than 340,000 passengers were stuck, unable to fly home or to their holidays.

The good news is that Jakarta's airport has now reopened. To help clear the backlog of stranded travellers, Singapore Airlines (SIA) added eight extra 'relief' flights between Singapore and Jakarta on Tuesday — four flights each way.

These extra flights depend on how many empty seats are available, so not everyone waiting will get a seat straight away. Still, it's a big help for families trying to get back to Singapore or reach Indonesia for work or holidays.
This shows how something happening far away, like a volcano erupting, can still affect plans right here in Singapore — especially if your family loves to travel to nearby countries.

lenses.me: If your family has a trip to Indonesia planned soon, it's worth checking with the airline in case of delays.
lenses.family: Families with holiday or work trips to Jakarta may need backup plans in case flights get rescheduled.
lenses.friends: A classmate's family holiday could be affected if they were flying through Jakarta this week.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singapore's airlines step in quickly to help travellers when disasters strike nearby countries.
lenses.world: It's a reminder that natural events like volcanic eruptions can disrupt travel across an entire region, not just one country.

stories.title: War in the Middle East Grows Bigger — Why It Could Affect Petrol Prices Here
stories.headline_kid: Fighting in the Middle East has spread to more cities, and it could make fuel more expensive around the world, including in Singapore.
summary: There is a war happening in the Middle East, a region far from Singapore but very important because many countries there produce oil, which is used to make petrol. This week, the fighting got bigger and more serious.

A group called the Houthis, based in Yemen and supported by Iran, attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia. Sadly, more than 70 people were hurt, and some oil facilities caught fire. In response, American forces struck several Iranian oil tankers (ships that carry oil).

This matters because a lot of the world's oil passes through this region on ships. When fighting breaks out near important shipping routes, oil companies get worried, and oil prices can go up. Singapore does not have its own oil, so we buy fuel from other countries — meaning higher oil prices can eventually make petrol and even bus or taxi fares more expensive here.

Grown-ups around the world are watching closely to see if the fighting spreads further, because it affects not just people living there, but businesses and families everywhere who rely on oil for cars, factories, and even the plastic in our toys.

lenses.me: If petrol prices go up, your parents might notice it costs more to fill up the family car.
lenses.family: Households may need to budget more carefully if fuel and transport costs rise.
lenses.friends: Your friends' families who drive or take grab rides may also feel the pinch if fares increase.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports almost all its fuel, so problems overseas can affect prices at home.
lenses.world: The conflict shows how events in one region can ripple out and affect economies and families everywhere.

stories.title: Nepal Flood: Sad News on Deaths, But Two Men Found Alive After 9 Days
stories.headline_kid: Nearly two weeks after a huge glacier collapse caused terrible floods in Nepal, rescuers found two men alive in a flooded tunnel — after nine days trapped in the dark.
summary: On 26 August, a giant chunk of glacier and mountain collapsed near the border of Nepal and China. It crashed into a river, causing a massive flood that swept away roads, bridges, and homes. It is now Nepal's worst flood disaster in decades.
Rescue teams have been searching non-stop for 14 days. Sadly, the death toll has now risen to 1,357 people, with more than 5,000 still missing. In China, 43 people died and hundreds more are missing.

Some workers were trapped underground when the flood buried the entrances of tunnels used for hydropower projects (places that make electricity from flowing water). Rescuers have been digging through mud and debris to reach them.

There was a moment of hope this week: two men, including one named Kabir Maharjan, were found alive after being trapped for nine days in complete darkness inside a flooded tunnel. Their survival gave rescuers new determination to keep searching for others.

lenses.me: It reminds me to be thankful for safety and to think about how scary it must be to be trapped somewhere dark for days.
lenses.family: Families can talk about ways to help, like donating to disaster relief funds.
lenses.friends: Classmates might discuss how communities around the world come together to help disaster victims.
lenses.nation: Singapore has sent help before, including police support, showing how countries can support each other in tough times.
lenses.world: The disaster shows how powerful nature can be, and why countries need good plans to warn people and rescue them quickly.

stories.title: Singaporean Admits Role in Huge $260 Million Online Crime
stories.headline_kid: A 22-year-old Singaporean has admitted to leading a group that stole more than $260 million worth of digital money from people online.
summary: Malone Lam, a 22-year-old Singaporean, has pleaded guilty in a United States court to leading a crime ring that stole more than US$260 million (about S$340 million) in cryptocurrency. Cryptocurrency is a type of digital money that exists only online, kept safe using special codes.

Lam admitted to organising the group, which tricked people who owned large amounts of cryptocurrency into giving up access to their digital wallets, then stole their money. This is called a 'racketeering conspiracy' — a fancy way of saying he led a criminal team.
Because the crime happened in the US and involved victims there, Lam is being punished under American law. He now faces up to 20 years in prison — that's longer than most of our lifetimes so far!

This case is a reminder that online crimes can happen anywhere, and that being careful with passwords, digital wallets, and personal information is important, whether you're an adult or a child using devices at home.

lenses.me: It reminds me to never share passwords or personal information with strangers online, even in games or apps.
lenses.family: Families should talk about staying safe online and recognising scams together.
lenses.friends: Classmates should be careful about clicking suspicious links or sharing account details, even for gaming accounts.
lenses.nation: It shows that even young Singaporeans can get involved in serious crimes, and highlights the importance of digital literacy education.
lenses.world: Online crime doesn't need borders — someone in one country can steal from victims anywhere in the world using the internet.

stories.title: Michael Jackson Musical 'MJ' Is Coming to Singapore in 2027!
stories.headline_kid: Get ready to moonwalk! A musical about the King of Pop, Michael Jackson, will open in Singapore next year.
summary: MJ The Michael Jackson Musical will open in Singapore in August 2027 at Sands Theatre, Marina Bay Sands. It's a show that tells the story of how Michael Jackson, one of the most famous singers and dancers ever, created his 1992 Dangerous World Tour.

The musical is told through the eyes of a journalist from MTV (a music TV channel) who is given special access to watch Jackson rehearse and prepare for his big tour. Along the way, the show features many of Jackson's biggest hit songs.

Jackson, often called the 'King of Pop', was famous for songs like Thriller and Beat It, as well as his incredible dance moves, including the moonwalk. This musical has already been a huge hit in cities like London and New York.
For Singapore fans of music and theatre, this is an exciting chance to see a world-famous show performed live, right here at home, without having to travel overseas.

lenses.me: If you enjoy music, dance, or theatre, this could be a fun show to watch with your family.
lenses.family: Families who love musicals might plan a special outing to watch MJ together in 2027.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could talk about your favourite Michael Jackson songs or dance moves.
lenses.nation: It shows Singapore continuing to attract big international shows, making it an exciting place for arts and culture.
lenses.world: It's part of a growing trend of world-famous musicals touring Asia, connecting audiences everywhere through music.
